hook_scenario: A brilliant, flawless presenter spills coffee all over his shirt, and suddenly everyone in the room likes him twice as much.
core_concept: Competent people become significantly more likable and relatable when they make a small, clumsy mistake.

hook_scenario: You walk into an office wearing a stained shirt convinced everyone is staring at you, but almost nobody even noticed.
core_concept: We intuitively overestimate how much other people notice our flaws, appearance, and awkward moments.

hook_scenario: Someone who watched a single 10-minute tutorial argues passionately with an expert who has practiced for fifteen years.
core_concept: People with low knowledge in a domain severely overestimate their competence, while genuine experts tend to doubt themselves.

hook_scenario: Give someone two months to complete a simple presentation and it takes exactly two months; give them two days and it gets done in two days.
core_concept: Work automatically expands to fill the exact time allocated for its completion.

hook_scenario: A teacher is falsely told that five random students are secret geniuses; by the end of the semester, those five students test higher than everyone else.
core_concept: Higher expectations placed on people lead directly to an increase in their actual performance.

hook_scenario: A vacation filled with delayed flights and rainy days is remembered fondly forever simply because of an incredible dinner on the final night.
core_concept: Humans judge past experiences based almost entirely on the emotional peak and how the experience ended, ignoring duration.

hook_scenario: A waiter remembers complex unpaid diner orders perfectly from memory, but completely forgets them seconds after the bill is paid.
core_concept: Our brains keep uncompleted or interrupted tasks top of mind while discarding finished ones.

hook_scenario: The government offers a cash reward for every dead cobra turned in to eliminate pests; instead, citizens begin breeding cobras for income.
core_concept: Incentives designed to solve a problem often unintentionally worsen the exact problem they aimed to fix.

hook_scenario: A supermarket table offering 24 jam flavors attracts huge crowds but almost no sales, while a table with just 6 flavors sells out instantly.
core_concept: Having too many options increases decision fatigue, paralysis, and post-purchase regret.

hook_scenario: Nobody buys a medium popcorn until the cinema prices it at $6.50 next to a large for $7.00, making the large seem like a steal.
core_concept: Introducing an asymmetrically dominated third option changes customer preference between the original two options.

hook_scenario: A family drives four hours through dust and heat to eat at a bad cafeteria in Abilene, only to discover afterwards that none of them wanted to go.
core_concept: A group collectively decides on a course of action that no individual member truly wanted, because each member wrongly assumed everyone else did.

hook_scenario: Engineers reinforce armor where returning bombers have bullet holes, until a mathematician points out the fallen planes were hit where returning planes have no holes.
core_concept: Focusing only on the successful survivors causes severe misjudgment by ignoring the unseen failures.
